items.stem: What happens when you send a message to nil in Objective-C, for example [nilObject doSomething]?

options.text: Nothing happens and the expression returns nil/zero, with no crash
options.rationale: Correct: messaging nil is a no-op that yields nil or zero, a defining Objective-C behaviour.

options.text: The program always crashes with a null-pointer error
options.rationale: Unlike a C null dereference, messaging nil is safe in Objective-C.

options.text: The message is queued until the object becomes non-nil
options.rationale: There is no queuing; the message is simply ignored.
It compiles and runs; the runtime handles nil.

items.explanation: Correct: messaging nil is a no-op that yields nil or zero, a defining Objective-C behaviour.

items.stem: Which statements about memory management under ARC are correct? (Select TWO)

options.text: A weak reference does not keep its target alive and is set to nil when the target is deallocated
options.rationale: Correct: weak avoids ownership and is zeroed automatically on deallocation.

options.text: Two objects holding strong references to each other can form a retain cycle
options.rationale: Correct: mutual strong references prevent deallocation, leaking memory.

options.text: Under ARC you must still call retain and release manually
options.rationale: ARC inserts retain/release automatically; manual calls are disallowed.
strong keeps the target alive; weak does not.

items.explanation: Correct: weak avoids ownership and is zeroed automatically on deallocation.; Correct: mutual strong references prevent deallocation, leaking memory.

items.stem: What does a category add to an existing Objective-C class?

options.text: Additional methods to the class without subclassing it
options.rationale: Correct: a category extends an existing class with new methods at runtime.

options.text: New instance variables guaranteed to be stored
options.rationale: Categories cannot add stored instance variables safely; they add methods.

options.text: A separate copy of the class hierarchy
options.rationale: A category modifies the existing class, not a copy.
Categories add methods, not just constants.

items.explanation: Correct: a category extends an existing class with new methods at runtime.
